The hard-disk phase-transition scenario, which has been under study for nearly five decades, was once thought to be infinitely transcendentally complex and thus unreachable for precise calculation.  Within this work, we provide an alternative perspective on its inherently complex nature.  15 years ago, we started a new, data-driven approach to investigating how the hard-disk model's equilibrium nature changes.  25 years later, we have obtained an unprecedented level of accuracy in our results.  Here, we explain the foundation and key findings of our research, as well as discuss the nature of its complexity.  We also present data that support or contradict earlier hypotheses concerning the critical exponent and value of the hard-disk phase transition.  Furthermore, we outline the current limitations of our approach and outline future directions for refinement.  The core hypothesis we put forward is that the hard-disk phase transition belongs to a simple, well-defined group.

This study explores the impact of nuclear parton distribution functions on the
interpretation of jet data from proton--nucleus and nucleus--nucleus
collisions, and how this affects the interpretation of jet structure, and it
proposes a method to quantify the modification of jet substructure in these
collisions, and compares the predicted multi-fractional jet moments to experimental data from nucleus--nucleus and proton--nucleus collisions, and it concludes that the jet data can be interpreted in part through the adjustment of jet cross-sections, but a more in-depth analysis of jet substructure is necessary to fully understand the interactions within the quark--gluon plasma, and it suggests that the initial jet splitting process is not the primary factor determining a jet's substructure, which supports the idea that N-subjet find tags are relatively insensitive to the energy scale, and it demonstrates that nucleus--nucleus and proton--nucleus collisions exhibit similar patterns, which indicates that the nucleus affects the parton density at the beginning of the collision, and it compares the predictions of two different nuclear parton distribution functions, and it finds that the quark--gluon momentum ratio is largely independent of the energy scale, which indicates that jet substructure data is a crucial input for parton distribution function models.

Investors in the cryptocurrency pyramidal scheme known as "Forsage" have reported monetary losses exceeding $500 million yet studies on pyramid schemes in the cryptocurrency market have largely overlooked these investors. Our research aims to rectify this gap by conducting an in-depth analysis of the risks investors face when participating in Forsage. Our findings reveal that nearly 99% of investors end up with losses and some have even lost nearly all their funds. Our data indicates that the vast majority (88%) of investors lose nearly or more than ten times their expected returns and over 80% lose more than 10 times their expected gains. Our study also discovers the link between the time spent investing and both total losses and success rates, and highlights the critical need for exchange platforms to shut down high-risk cryptocurrencies like the one used by Forsage.

We have developed the age distribution of the Milky Way's globular cluster population using researchers' estimated ages. So far, the age distribution is mainly confined within 13 billion years due to many young clusters being missing. In the field of astrophysics, three potential globular cluster candidates have been identified that may fill the gap between 8.3 and 10.2 billion years. A specific object, which was initially thought to be an intermediate mass black hole, has since been reclassified as a globular cluster based on its spectral analysis. When analyzing the OII line, the object exhibits characteristics of an early-type globular cluster. It is also significantly less luminous and more compact than Sgr GCs, which are known to consist of multiple clusters. Our investigation indicates a gap in the Milky Way's cluster age distribution and a possible explanation for the so-called "10 Gyr sequence gap" that has been observed in the Sgr RC. We are using the Hubble Space Telescope to verify the nature of this specific object with higher precision. It is also possible that there are numerous similar objects that are misclassified as IMBHs, representing the sequence gap-filling "10 Gyr sequence" that has been observed in the Sgr RC.

This study examines the impact of virtual Higgs boson production in quark-antiquark annihilation on the total cross section in quark scattering at high energy levels, taking into consideration the nonperturbative hadronization of off-shell quarks through a thermal quark mass mechanism, which was previously investigated in connection with the J/$\psi$-nucleon total cross section. We analyze the influence of the quark mass effects on the transverse momentum distribution and we find that the distribution behaves similarly to a Gaussian curve, with the parameter $<p_{T}^{2}>$ determined mainly by the temperature $T$, with an approximate value of $<p_{T}^{2}> \approx (3/5) \cdot T^{2}$. We also examine the impact of virtual Higgs branching and discover that it has a minimal effect on the peak value of the distribution.

We develop a global current operator for tight-binding models that are Desiderio-type, tackling a well-known limitation in a specific type of model used to simulate materials. The model, which accurately describes a material's interaction with light across a wide range of frequencies, particularly for insulators, takes into consideration various factors such as saturation effects, the transfer of momentum between electrons and lattice, and different types of polarization. To arrive at this refined model, we employ a first-principles approach, leveraging a path-ordered expansion in a external field to identify key terms in the beginning and middle regimes. The results from this derivation are confirmed by a field-theoretic approach using coherent states, providing a underlying mathematical framework for coherent-state DFT. The obtained expression for the current in the velocity gauge can also be used as a starting point for describing a material's response to strong laser fields.

A network of tensors can represent a quantum state's density matrix in the form of a telescopic product, potentially serving as an error-correction code against information loss. If such a network consists of a single type of tensor, strict limitations are imposed: the quantum code cannot emulate certain types of symmetries, like global U(1) charges, and its ability to correct errors is limited due to the inherent constraints of the tensor network's structure. As an alternative, we have developed a code that has a uniform structure network which can global U(1) charges and local electric field measurements while preserving the ability to correct such losses. This code has a network which has a single type of tensor and has a larger density matrix than the toric code, and we have demonstrated that it has a uniformity property which does not rely on a specific graph structure, and we have established conditions under which this general framework can achieve a quantum code that has a uniformity.

This study investigates the long-standing query concerning the role of
quantum yield stability in condensed-phase photochemistry, biological light
sensing, and light-driven processes. We quantify this relationship by linking
the quantum yield to the depth of a potential energy well and its curvature,
which can be readily measured or simulated. These findings imply that an
absolutely quantum yield insensitive system may yet serve a functional role.
Notably, this requirement can be met when a well becomes shallower at an
excited state minimum/flat region, which can be anisotropic and thus has
implications for light sensing due to its wavelength dependence.

As businesses increasingly generate digital data, there's growing interest in forecasting event occurrences within processes. Existing research utilizes various approaches, using different datasets and evaluation metrics, making cross-method comparison challenging. This study leverages the large car rental dataset from Spaghetti Flow to clarify the prediction problem and assess existing models. It identifies two key factors affecting results: dataset characteristics and metric selection. Due to the large scale of typical process mining datasets, minor errors can significantly impact evaluation. A novel adaptive metric is proposed to mitigate this issue. Experimental results show that changing from a global to a local assessment leads to distinct outcome variations, with some previously best-performing models experiencing significant declines. Furthermore, factors like changes in process structure and seasonality can drastically affect outcomes. This study's findings imply that process predictions should not be made without considering their practical applications, as performance can vary significantly across different contexts.

Earthquakes and other major disasters have left indelible marks on people's feelings, but measuring these changes from Earth orbit has been largely unachievable.  However, given the significant impact of public sentiment on human behavior and consequent strain on disaster-affected regions, it becomes crucial to assess public feelings quickly following major events using geospatial social media data via NLP techniques. This study analyzes the changes in sentiment towards Earth from geospatial Twitter data following three significant events, including the 2019 Japan Earthquake, and reveals an measurable shift in sentiment towards Japan on Twitter following the earthquake, an finding that is hard to explain from an emotional perspective. It is also hard to overlook the limitations and difficulties associated with carrying out such studies. This research aims to set a baseline for future geological science and social science research that combine scientific analysis with in-depth textual understanding.

This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the Gelfand-Shilov spaces S^σ_σ, with σ belonging to (0,1), by examining the characteristics of their Fourier transforms. Key features of functions within these specific spaces can be better understood, and practical tests established to identify functions that belong to them.

We analyzed changes in hydrogen spectral line broadening, optical and far-ultraviolet continuum properties during 17 X-ray and 5 optical stellar flares. A correlation was found between Minimum Broadening Time (MBT) and a parameter $E_{\rm cut}$ characterizing the energy distribution of electrons responsible for continuum emission, with shorter MBT associated with more optically bright flares. The electron distribution cut-off energy $E_{\rm cut}$ also explains the observed relationship between flare line broadening and continuum brightness. We propose that line broadening is a result of magnetic reconnection in the stellar atmosphere, while the optical and far-ultraviolet continuum emission originates from magnetic reconnection in the stellar atmosphere.

This study explores nonlinear directed propagation in a unique scenario where a wave can directed propagate in a system exhibiting symmetry breaking due to nonlinearity, preceding the symmetry breaking induced by linear effects. Using a detailed mathematical model and numerical simulations, we investigate this phenomenon with a specific model: a one-dimensional periodic structure that features a forward and backward waveguide and demonstrates point symmetry nonlinearity. We analyze this system with a transfer matrix approach, demonstrating that in a unit cell that is off-resonance, there is an asymmetric critical amplitude where directed propagation is achieved. Conversely, as this amplitude approaches its critical point, the directed propagation amplitude is almost equal to the broken phase amplitude. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an ensemble of such unit cells can exhibit similar directed propagation amplitudes and that this effect can be utilized for designing nonlinear optical diodes with significantly lower threshold amplitudes.

We extend the existing dynamical cavity method, developed for linear and Boolean networks, to accommodate a quadratic self-interaction within an asymmetric configuration. This extension allows us to calculate a cavity generating function for a specific class of signals and determine a cavity order parameter. This calculation is feasible thanks to a suitable transformation of the network dynamics, which we perform for a quadratic self-interaction. This method is straightforward to apply and yields a closed equation, which we use to evaluate the long-term average activity within the network.

Quantum mechanics corrections linked to the 1/v expansion can be used to understand and enhance the apparent restoration of symmetries within complex nuclear systems. Considering the extensive and detailed data available for nuclear matter, it becomes possible to derive precise lower bounds, specifically for systems with an extensive radius, there is an enhanced chance of observing complete chiral and flavor symmetries within excited states. This hypothesis can ultimately be validated through an in-depth examination of the corresponding invariant masses in a thorough analysis of decay patterns.

Continuous Wave Frequency Modulation (FMCW) radar networks provide several crucial advantages, including the ability to measure range and velocity simultaneously, along with notable advantages. To take full advantage of this technology, research needs to be focused on its planning and design. However, currently, there is not enough knowledge about its planning, impelling the development of analytical models tailored for FMCW-based applications. In this research, a novel analytical model is created to calculate interference probabilities, accounting for varying numbers of chirps per signal, and its accuracy is confirmed through computer simulations. The model is further utilized to develop an optimal counting method for chirps per message, which can enhance performance. Notably, as the number of chirps per message increases, there is a notable improvement in performance, even up to a 50% greater throughput compared to fewer chirps, observed in both theoretical models and simulation tests.

This paper addresses the challenge of predicting missing information in knowledge graphs that evolve over time by introducing a novel encoding method called cycle-aware time-encoding. This approach captures both regular patterns and complex changes in dynamics by incorporating a coarse-grained detail-aware time-encoding mechanism and a circular time-embedding layer. Additionally, we propose a triple representation fusion method called low-high interaction to leverage details and broader patterns through an low-high interaction. Furthermore, we enhance our model with a gradual interaction attention mechanism to differentially weigh triple components and entity relationships. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of our proposed method through performance comparisons and logical analysis.

To investigate the characteristics of the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, an in-depth analysis was conducted within the Relativistic Particle-Hole Approximation framework, supported by the relativistic energy density functional Hamada-Johnston-Uchiya parameter set. A comprehensive examination of pole structures, determined through the long-range metric transformation method, was carried out to compare with a set of $19$ distinct potential models. Furthermore, an exploration of the relationship between the pole structures of $^{16}$O and its heavier analogue $^{28}$Si was conducted within the same theoretical framework. A rigorous demonstration was provided to confirm that the photon operator does not disrupt the completeness of the particle-hole basis used to define the pole energies and corresponding wave functions. A complete set of particle-hole excitations, exceeding the limitations of previous studies, was employed in these analyses.

We explore a framework for studying nonlinear dynamical systems using the Koopman operator. This approach allows us to employ linear system theory and handle complex, nonlinear dynamics by analyzing an infinite-dimensional linear system formed by observable functions. Although there are well-established methods for approximating the Koopman operator and framing it within a stochastic differential equation context, there is not yet a established way to use these approaches to compute a frame pullback operator corresponding to a Koopman operator approximated via the Hamming distance. In this study, we derive an approximation of this pullback operator and investigate its connection to the approximate Koopman operator and the underlying dynamical system.

Neural text generation models typically struggle with capturing a sentence's overall structure and individual word dependencies. To address this issue, we propose SparseGAN, a method that integrates structural information into the representation learning process for text. By utilizing a gan to encode and decode sentence representations, we discover a sparse adjacency matrix that captures the dependency patterns in a corpus. We then apply this matrix to refine the representation learning process, combining self-representation with structural gains. Our approach outpermodels current state-of-the-art techniques on multiple evaluation metrics in various generation tasks, demonstrating its ability to enhance both the accuracy and efficiency of neural text generation.

We investigate how foreground signal subtraction, specifically for CMB and Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect data, influences the accuracy of cosmological parameter estimation using a realistic Bayesian model comparison approach. Employing the NEXUS simulation package and full marginalization in analysis, we compare the effects of different foreground removal methods on parameter inference. Our study reveals that the current foreground subtraction algorithm implemented in Commapte can introduce biases of up to $3\sigma$ for certain parameters, primarily due to residual foreground contamination rather than an imperfect model. Newer foreground removal algorithms are anticipated to mitigate this contamination and enhance the estimation's reliability. Additionally, our analysis highlights the feasibility of distinguishing between cosmological models, with the ability to confidently rule out alternatives at greater than $5\sigma$ confidence levels, given a full sky map with angular power spectrum resolution of $\ell \lesssim 2000$.

In the proposed quintessential dark matter model, dark matter fields are made up of distinct components, similar to how an oscillating dark matter field can be divided into high and low energy states.  According to this model, the less energetic state behaves like traditional slow-rolling dark matter, whereas the more energetic state represents a rapidly fluctuating component that makes up only a small fraction of the total dark matter.  This fast-fluctuating component may offer an alternative explanation for the observed 5-sigma anomaly in the long-range five-fold correlation of the cosmic microwave background.

A spatial capture-recapture model was developed to estimate population density based on capture events of individual animals over time, where the activity domain may vary between capture occasions. This particular model addresses the issue of activity domain variation, which is commonly observed in ecological studies involving the control release of live traps. It assumes that the activity domain for each capture occasion follows a specific distribution determined by the proportion of total trap nights dedicated to that particular occasion. This model offers a more accurate estimation of population density and its associated standard error, which is seen as a prerequisite for conducting cost-benefit analyses of capture efforts. To test its assumptions, data was generated from a known activity domain for each capture occasion, and the model's parameter estimates were compared with those of the true values. The model's density and its coefficient of variation matched those of the true values, which confirmed its accuracy. This model could be utilized to analyze the impact of allocating trap nights across different locations and could also be applied when trap placements differ between capture occasions.

We examine the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, a challenging variant of determining the minimum total weight of k edge-disjoint st-paths in a graph, where each edge's influence on the problem is defined by a power of its weight in a given r-function. If a graph has multiple possible weights for its edges, this problem arises from network design, with the goal of connecting k sources to a destination using the least energy. We show that for any given integer k greater than one, the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem is NP-complete, and specifically for binary weight graphs (r=1), we develop an $O(2^k \cdot n)$ time algorithm. Additionally, we propose a new algorithm with $O(n \cdot \sqrt{n} \cdot \log n)$ time, which for bivalent graphs (r=2), improves on a previous algorithm by Dou and Hou (Inform. Process. Lett. 107, 2009) and the general algorithm by Zelikovsky et al. (Algorithmica 29, 2001).

A labeled filter using the Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli method has been proven
effective for tracking multiple targets, and this work extends that approach by
addressing the issue of assigning labels to untracked targets. To achieve this, a
new algorithm is introduced - the Generalized Association-PNHCT, which integrates the
Not-Means hypothesis from the Labeled Multi-Bernoulli framework with an imperfect
measurement model. The proposed algorithm's performance is evaluated through
simulation tests, and the results demonstrate its tracking capability, however,
it is found that the label management strategy using association labels can lead to
fragmentation of labels in the posterior distribution, and a new condition is derived
to predict this behavior.

We examine the dynamics of an $s$-bootstrap percolation process on a network that has been randomly damaged, where the requirement for a node to be reactivated increases with the fraction of removed nodes on its surrounding perimeter. Choosing a starting configuration of active nodes at random and denoting the minimum required degree as $m$, the model mimics a disease that spreads through a network while simultaneously causing a certain proportion of nodes and their connections to disappear. If the required number increases rapidly, there is a sudden, unanticipated change in a complex network where the prevalence of an infectious condition and the probability of a connection remaining intact both follow a power-law pattern at a critical starting configuration size; this exponent is influenced by the underlying structure of the network. Notably, a x-network shows a direct correlation between the two patterns. Leveraging a simple scaling law, we derive a universal relation between the two patterns that applies across various network models including y-meshes. Furthermore, we investigate a y-Mesh network and find that a complex network can exhibit a delocalized state that covers a large area.

A critical aspect of modern football strategy involves anticipating an opponent's likelihood of gaining possession, prompting the development of an innovative predictive model. In addition, a novel football scoring model introduces an uncharted approach to predicting game outcomes, which, despite its potential, has yet to find widespread adoption due to various external factors. To overcome these challenges, measuring a player's 'skill level' becomes pivotal, which can be effectively achieved through data that remains consistent across different teams and competitions. Furthermore, this effect can be isolated by analyzing an individual's performance relative to their teammates during a specific match.

In real-world scenarios, documents often contain various levels of noise, which can significantly interfere with the system's ability to accurately identify connections between text. To overcome this challenge, we incorporated control inputs into our neural network model, enabling it to discern various levels of background noise in images. Based on the noise detection capability, the network automatically adjusts the complexity of its text connection analysis sub-model. Experimental evidence shows that this adaptive approach significantly enhances the model's ability to identifying text connections in noisy documents. We assessed the proposed model's performance using a large dataset consisting of 12,000 noisy document images. To accelerate training, we developed a novel data augmentation technique called super-positioned noise, which simulates the effects of various levels of background noise. This innovative augmentation method enables the model to efficiently learn from a diverse range of noise representations. As a result, it achieves comparable performance to applying different noise reduction algorithms, but at a much lower computational cost and without the need for extra post-processing steps.

We have developed a new model called Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs) that effectively captures complex system dynamics by introducing variable parameters between time steps. These hidden parameters form their own structure as temporal intervals affect a complex entanglement in the feature space. Both the model and inference components have been trained using variational methods, allowing for unconstrained optimization. We have successfully applied a learning algorithm based on random gradient methods to minimize the discrepancy between predicted and observed data, as well as reduce the variance of the estimated features. Our model enables an unbounded state space, eliminating the need for tangent linearizations commonly found in flow-based models. In addition, it introduces discrete latent variables that are difficult to model with continuous approaches. Our model allows for a smoother and continuous probability distribution, making it easier to handle such variables.

This study delves into the conditions of conditional freeness within the framework of random matrix theory, establishing new results that reveal the incompatibility of conditional freeness and Nairn symmetry when considering large systems, ultimately deriving consequences such as the determination of empirical spectral distribution. A key aspect involves analyzing the conditioning event's impact on a random matrix's eigenvalues, with conditionally free summands exhibiting similar behavior under certain limitations, which can later be exploited to investigate specific properties of large alternating sign matrices.

Let $C$ be a non-hyperelliptic curve of genus 3 with a point $p$. If we take the preimage of $p$, which consists of two points $\{q_1, q_2\}$ in a genus 1 curve $E$ that is covered by $C$, then $C$ covers $E$. We show that if we remove $q_1$ and $q_2$ from $C$ and a point from $E$, then we can lift the covering of $E$ by $C-\{q_1, q_2\}$ to a covering of a genus 2 curve by the product of $E$ and an elliptic curve. We also provide a parametric description of the genus 2 curves in terms of the parameters of $C$ and $E$.

The study of polarization on the internet has gained significant attention, yet the research community still lacks a clear understanding of which methods yield the most relevant results. Previous attempts to address this issue have focused chiefly on specific contexts, such as US elections. In contrast, our research takes a broader approach by examining a diverse array of networks and elections across different countries, including parliamentary elections, local elections, and even the political landscape of Israel. We analyze existing measurement methods with a critical eye, assessing their suitability for capturing polarization. Our findings led to the development of a novel, general approach that accounts for various factors, ultimately revealing a striking inconsistency in the results obtained using previous methods. Moreover, our new approach produced results that diverge significantly from those of the current state-of-the-art method.

We investigate a method to compute and determine the stability of multiple states in a complex network structure that consists of interconnected layers. Utilizing a technique called a linear stability matrix, we can efficiently assess the stability of different configurations without solving the full problem for each individual case. Our approach leverages a transformation matrix that connects the stability matrices of adjacent layers, enabling a significant reduction in computational effort. This method is particularly effective for large, periodically structured networks, where we only need to calculate and store the stability matrices for a small number of layers. We demonstrate this efficiency by analyzing a commonly studied model known as the Complex Networked Kuramoto model. However, our technique has broader implications and can be applied to a wide range of models, including those used in physics and other fields.

Given two differential modules M and N over the ring K{\theta}, we say $\Gamma$ is parameterized by $\Delta$ if the solution space of $\Gamma$ is contained in the solution space of $\Delta$. In this paper, we establish a criterion for when one Euler operator $t-\theta$ is parameterized by another, showing that this occurs if and only if the modules $M$ and $N$ are isomorphic. Furthermore, we extend this result to multiple Euler operators, demonstrating that the condition is met if and only if there is a specific form of non-degenerate pairing between two sub-modules of $M$. This study is relevant to identifying hypergeometric differential operators $\Theta$ with solution spaces identical to those of a given operator $\Delta$.

Our research identifies a pivotal role for the testing environment and its
feedback mechanisms in facilitating the location and correction of bugs by
users. We have developed an innovative, self-operating algorithm within the
testing environment that can pinpoint and pin down buggy code segments, as well
as modify them to fix issues. Our experiments revealed that this algorithm
effectively pinpoints buggy code in more than nine out of ten instances, as
well as correctly modifies bugs in around 60% of cases. Moreover, our findings
show that the algorithm's code modification success rate is significantly
higher compared to other commonly used techniques for modifying buggy code, such
as altering an if statement, changing a comparison operator, or adjusting a
literal value.

Recent research in the field of Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision has been heavily influenced by Prompt Tuning techniques, which involve adjusting pre-trained models through the modification of input prompts or the insertion of task-specific modules like Cross Attention. Building on this research, we introduce HyperPrompt, a method that employs HyperNetworks to generate task-adaptive modules from pre-trained networks. Specifically, we demonstrate how HyperNetworks can be used to encode task embeddings and generate Cross Attention modules by transforming parts of the BERT backbone. Experiments conducted on the GLUE benchmark show improved performance over previous results, particularly on tasks requiring logical reasoning. Additionally, we achieve comparable performance to full BERT while reducing the model size by 15x, indicating significant gains in model efficiency.

Consider the simple root system $\Phi$ in an $l$-dimensional Euclidean space, along with its associated integral weight system $\Lambda$. For the cases $A_l$ and $D_l$, we define a special root $\mu$ by combining the fundamental weights with specific integer coefficients. This paper demonstrates that for these root systems, the maximal root $\mu$ has desirable properties: it is reduced by only a single integer to yield a sum of positive roots, and also by a related formula to produce the same sum of roots. This paper also establishes a connection between $\mu$ and a particularly extreme combinatorial object within the Weyl group, and that connection can be simplified to resolve long-standing conjectures by Fock-Chen and Garfinkle.

We propose a novel design based on a double split-rotator configuration, comprising two highly excited atomic states and two ground states, for producing even and odd correlated photons from a cavity QED setup. By adjusting the coupling between the excited and ground states, we demonstrate the ability to control the emission of even or odd correlated photons. Additionally, we show that this control can be achieved rapidly. Our design offers optimal qualities for even and odd correlated photons, including a high Jahnell parameter of 0.93, a low Quesnaire parameter of 0.07, and long lifetimes of 32 ns and 2.5 $\mu$s, respectively, making it suitable for the secure distribution of quantum information.

Our algorithm for estimating the total number of items in a count network requires only count information from each node, contrasting with our previous methods that needed stored coordinates. We've developed a novel, efficiently scalable algorithm applicable to modern data centers and social network platforms. Our method employs an innovative randomized distribution approach that significantly reduces computation time, involving the generation of randomly selected subsets and a simplified estimation formula. We've created a specialized algorithm for its implementation that further enhances scalability by eliminating the need for centralized storage. Our randomized approach has been proven effective, yielding accurate results with minimal variance, and our algorithm successfully handles counts up to $10^{14}$ with an average error under 1%.

A novel approach for nonparametric estimation of network queue lengths is presented, which achieves superior accuracy over traditional parametric methods. This estimation serves as a key input for active queue management systems, ensuring their effective operation. We have developed a new estimator that does not rely on assumptions about underlying probability distributions and demonstrates remarkable robustness. The study involves simulations and real-world experiments to test the performance of this method, showing that it closely aligns with theoretically predicted results. Furthermore, the paper addresses issues related to queue length values that fall below zero and proposes modifications to address these challenges.

We investigate a novel approach to handling the Hamiltonian constraint in gravity simulations, where we treat the conformal factors as independent variables from the metric's remaining components. This new method avoids parameterizing the potential based on excess matter density, which can create singularities. Instead, we develop a set of algebraic equations to solve for the conformal factors directly, method depends on a choice of gauge for the Einstein equations. By framing the problem this way, we ensure a root always exists, as long as the metric satisfies the momentum constraint. Furthermore, this approach enforces a specific behavior for the conformal factors, regardless of potential data irregularities, effectively filtering out short-wavelength distortions. We combine this method with a Newton iteration to ensure solution stability. The approach is tested on various scenarios, including smooth Schwarzschild and massless Bartnik configurations, a binary black hole merger simulation, and an initially irregular binary Bartnik configuration. The results show enhanced stability and accuracy in solving the Hamiltonian constraint compared to traditional methods. The method provides a robust alternative to traditional methods for solving the Hamiltonian constraint in numerical relativity simulations. By treating the conformal factors as independent variables, we avoid the use of an elliptic solver and instead express the conformal factor as a function of other variables based on the gauge choice for solving the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints. Unlike other potential-based approaches that model the potential in a specific way, this method does not assume a specific behavior for the potential. A root

The search for a rare $\Sigma^+ \to p \ell^0 \ell^0$ decay involving a lepton pair and a proton is being conducted, with either pions or photons as possible lepton alternatives. The expected and actual event counts from background processes are being compared, with stringent constraints placed on events exceeding one standard deviation. As a result, no evidence for $\Sigma^+ $ decay with photons has been found, nor any excess of events indicating a $\Sigma^+ $ decay with electrons.

We have examined the anormalous Nernst and Seebeck effects in two types of antiperovskites, $Fe_3Pt$ and $Co_3Pt$. By measuring Nernst and Seebeck coefficients at room temperature and a magnetic field of 9 T, we found that both materials, which have opposite polarities of their valence $p$-electrons, show the same positive signs for the Nernst and Seebeck coefficients. This discrepancy between the expected and observed results is addressed by detailed analyses. A mathematical model is also proposed to account for the observed thermoelectric and transport properties in these antiferromagnetic antiperovskites.

To tackle the scarcity of labels in web-scale supervised learning, we've developed an innovative training framework called Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE). By selectively utilizing label information, PILE dynamically adjusts the difficulty level of sample pairs and refines its predictions through self-feedback. Our method has achieved remarkable success, improving the existing Query-Click-Label (QCL) baseline AUC from 0.5624 to 0.616 on the Ms-MGCC test set, with an extensive dataset comprising 200 million training samples and only 3.5 million labels. To PILE's advantage, it doesn't rely on pre-trained models or complex optimization techniques like negative sampling, allowing for an entirely end-to-end training process.

Beam loss mechanisms in circular accelerators typically involve high-energy beam peeling off, unstable resonator modes, or gradual beam loss over time. In the case of the LHC, beam injection results in low-energy proton losses spread out, which are not a primary concern for the upstream neutral spallation target. The target's design is instead driven by the high-energy beam loss that occurs during a beam injection period, with a design beam loss of 3 TeV every 37.5 seconds and 37.5 minutes. Due to the significant beam loss during the injection process, a specialized beam loss monitor with exceptional sensitivity and a unique design are required. Furthermore, detecting this beam loss poses additional challenges as the target area is surrounded by a strong 8.36 T dipole magnetic field and the target itself contains several layers. Various monitor designs were evaluated, with the most suitable option being a multi-channel ferromagnetic lens solid-state beam loss monitor, which has very high sensitivity (1 W) and is not affected by the magnetic field. However, with a 6x10^7 protons per pulse and 450 ns beam pulse width, a special low gain readout circuit are required to avoid saturation. The target was designed to house the beam loss monitor at the most optimal location, with a custom-designed readout circuit placed in a special beam loss monitor position. The circuit has a particularly unique design with an ultra-low gain (10^-4)

A key driver of progress at user facilities like synchrotron light sources is innovation in experimental techniques. This often involves developing new methods and tools for investigation, which in turn can unlock new applications for the technique and the underlying technology. Given the substantial investment in these techniques, it is essential to allocate resources for research and development aimed at enhancing them. This includes supporting the efforts of both the user community and the operational staff to incorporate novel concepts and concepts for future uses. This could potentially be funded through the existing Light Source User Committee structure or a dedicated committee, with research and development projects receiving grants similar to those available through the National Science Foundation. This approach could include introducing new concepts to existing beamlines, exploring new applications for established techniques, and developing new beamlines based on cutting-edge concepts.

In the given paper, we provide a new bound for the entire solution to a specific type of mathematical problem known as a non-autonomous obstacle problem, under certain conditions and given specific constraints on a given surface. Our findings build on a previous result by Monneau but with an improved and more versatile approach. Additionally, our proof offers a alternative approach to two of monneau's original sub solutions comparison arguments.

A new explanation for the low sensitivity of Gamma Modes (GAMs) to the ratio of electron to ion temperature is proposed, which posits that a significant variation in the dispersion curve of GAMs observed in figure 1 of reference [10] occurs not at the location indicated in that figure, but rather corresponds to the inner curve seen in figure 2 of reference [10]. This switch in the dispersion curve's behavior is explained as a transition between two different asymptotic limits: the ion temperature asymptotic limit and the electron temperature asymptotic limit. Furthermore, it is concluded that the inner curve, which exists for high ratios of electron to ion temperature, exists for the entire range of the dispersion curve's electron temperature asymptotic limit and exists for the inner curve for lower ratios of electron to ion temperature. This conclusion is supported by the observation that the inner curve corresponds to the point where the dispersion curve transitions from its asymptotic limits, which occurs at the ratio of electron to ion temperature where the real frequency of GAMs is most sensitive to the ratio of electron to ion temperature, which is consistent with previous studies.

Typically, quantum annealing processes are hindered by environmental decoherence, but we show that for specific problems, it can be beneficial in overcoming energy barriers. We investigated the dynamics of quantum annealing with dissipation for a class of solvable models, based on a transverse-field Ising chain, where we determined the exact amplitude for being in the target ground state. We found the threshold for decoherence where a sudden drop in this success probability occurs. For problems involving ground states with fewer complex entanglement patterns, the threshold corresponds with a point where the system's internal structure most closely mirrors that of the environment, and it can be lowered by decreasing the strength of interaction between the system and environment. We also explored whether this finding extends to more complex scenarios not based on these models. Finally, we examined how this could impact using quantum annealing to solve one-dimensional optimization tasks.

In 1899, the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory was established in Leiden's astronomical department, but in 1923, it was moved to the University of Groningen. This move gave the laboratory independence from the Leiden institute, which had limited funds due to Kapteyn's high salary. Conversely, the move to Groningen resulted in increased funding and personal support for Kapteyn, as well as the opportunity to build a new observatory. However, this also led to a decrease in the laboratory's influence in the field of astronomy in Leiden. Although Kapteyn visited the observatory in Leiden and maintained the institute's involvement in the Kapteyn survey, his focus shifted to other pursuits, and his influence in Leiden's astronomy department was largely confined to his student H. A. Lorentz.

We introduce a generalization of Kummer theory for both the p-primary series and its secondary, tertiary, and higher components. Specifically, we define and characterize G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles of various types, which represent extensions of the absolute Galois group of a field E, an algebraic closure of K, with a specified continuous action on the p-primary series. These cocycles arise naturally in the context of canonical filtrations on the extension, which include the projection from higher ARTIN-SCHEIER layers to the G_K-primary series, as well as the reduction modulo p of crystalline extensions of the absolute Galois group of K. Additionally, we establish a fundamental theorem for the ARTIN-SCHEIER complex in the second and third paragraphs.
We provide a new definition of flatness at a mesoscale level for a technical reason. This new definition can be used to study hypersurfaces in Euclidean space that have limited curvature.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) serve as powerful tools for feature extraction in optical flow estimation. Our proposed method, a efficient optimization technique, enhances training speed for various flow models by shifting the computation of a critic network's backward pass. This technique, local critic training (LCT), achieves an up to 4x speedup for commonly used flow models, making them competitive with state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we speed up the computation of a attention mechanism in one optical flow DNN model, resulting in an additional 1.6x speedup. The benefits of LCT are such that it accelerates the training of convolutional and recurrent neural networks, and our method's computational efficiency is such that is achieves an overall 2.5x speedup compared to current methods.

A novel approach to tackling the ill-posed nature of inverse problems in self-sensing composite structures has been successfully implemented using a genetic algorithm. The effectiveness of this method was validated through an application to a finite element model emulating a bonded fiber composite patch on an aluminum skin with various simulated damage scenarios. The model was calibrated to match the accuracy of experimental data obtained from real structures, and it demonstrated a significant improvement in damage detection accuracy compared to traditional optimization methods, particularly in terms of element failure rates. The use of a genetic algorithm resulted in a more precise damage representation, avoiding unnecessary structural breakdown and accurately emulating actual physical test outcomes.

To investigate the connection between various forms of cognition and dynamic relationships in biology, we have integrated different types of intelligence into the classic Lotka-Volterra model of biological interactions. This integration allows us to examine how nonlinear predessor-prey connections can lead to the effects of time-lagged population changes, ultimately influencing the co-existence, extinction, and oscillatory behavior of species through the application of a mathematical theorem that analyzes stability in cognitive systems. This analysis serves to highlight the significance of cognition in biological interactions and to map the parameters that lead to equilibrium behavior and oscillatory patterns, and it also demonstrates the critical role of cognition in ecological and evolutionary processes and the potential for different types of intelligence to produce distinct outcomes for species survival.

This research explores a novel learning-based control method that integrates linear matrix inequalities to enhance performance in scenarios with limited data, contrasting it to conventional reinforcement learning approaches. We theoretically prove that under optimal conditions, the new method matches or surpasses the efficacy of traditional techniques. To further validate its superiority, we develop an alternative formulation and evaluate results across multiple test cases. We also examine how gradually reducing the penalty term in the associated quadratic program, related to nominal control efficacy, impacts algorithm performance.

We propose an innovative method of applying geometric vector analysis to confirm a mathematical identity first established by a groundbreaking geometric proof. By combining geometric insights with mathematical calculations, we prove the identity of a mathematical equation. Additionally, we make significant progress on a related identity to ensure its validity.

To resolve the discrepancy between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements of the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, new experiments with a muon anomaly resolution as precise as $1.5 \times 10^{-7}$ are planned for the near future, specifically the Muon g-2 experiment at the Fermilab. The same level of precision can be achieved with intensity difference spectroscopy of muonium and antimuonium at a intensity difference spectroscopy facility. This paper outlines the parameter space for the muon g-2, dark matter interaction, and beyond the Standard Model physics that could be explored by a muon beam, and discusses the capabilities and potential of the proposed facility. The study demonstrates that the E6 at CERN and the proposed facility can significantly expand the parameter space for the muon g-2 and dark matter interaction, and probe several models, including the two-Higgs-doublet model and leptoquark models.

This paper analyzes Google App Engine data to explore how application development education impacts students in computer science, particularly those from under-represented minorities. It examines daily and monthly patterns in application development, exploring variations by time of day, day of week, month, and semester. Results show a significant application development surge during specific hours on weekdays, with peak activity occurring between 7-11am and 2-6pm Monday through Thursday. However, under-represented minority students did not exhibit the same engagement pattern, and their activity dropped by 50% on weekends compared to non-under-represented minorities who increased their activity. During the COVID-19 pandemic and the shift to remote learning, non-under-represented minorities showed the same engagement pattern on weekdays but exhibited significantly higher activity during evenings, late nights, and weekends. In contrast, under-represented minority students displayed no such pattern. Additionally, during the pandemic, applications developed by non-under-represented minorities shifted towards entertainment, while those developed by under-re-represented minorities were used for under-6 year olds, reflecting the need for under-supervised children to stay engaged. This analysis highlights the value of under-represented minorities in application development programs and the importance of considering their unique needs to create effective online learning experiences.

We examine the higher-spin symmetry of Toda conformal field theories in two-dimensional space by analyzing spin-three Ward identities specific to Toda CFT, making sure all details are thoroughly accounted for. 

By applying this approach, we derive a set of simplified constraints on the four-point functions of primary conformal fields in Toda CFT, under the assumption that the theory contains a spin-three primary. 

Furthermore, we demonstrate that the web of relationships defined by the Ward identities can be further reduced, and we show that they are intimately linked to the algebra of two-dimensional conformal field theory with spin-two symmetry. 

We also reveal a hidden correlation between the solvability of Toda CFT and its higher-spin symmetry, and we explore the implications of this relationship on the path integral formulation of Wess-Zumino-Witten model on a manifold whose dynamics are governed by a Toda theory. 

Consequently, we show that inserting a shockwave of stress-energy into a system of spin-two symmetry allows us to precisely calculate the change in gravitational entropy, and we demonstrate that this method yields the same result as the holographic correspondence in asymptotically Anti-de Sitter space.
We extend a previous finding by showing that all uniform lattices within fixed classical Lie groups and simple discrete transformation groups of a tree are biautomatic.

We investigate near-extremal and extremal Schwarzschild black holes scattered with a massless scalar field in both $4$ and $5$ dimensions to understand their final states after scattering. In our analysis, we examine both supercritical and subcritical cases. For near-extremal and extremal black holes in $4$ dimensions, we are able to trace the near horizon dynamics of the scalar field. However, in $5$ dimensions, we only have access to the asymptotic behavior at infinity for the scalar field. Our results show that when scalar field scattering reaches a critical threshold, the black hole transitions to a charged higher spin Reissner-Nordstrom black hole. In near-supracritical and sub-supracritical scenarios, there is no complete transition to a charged higher spin Reissner-Nordstrom black hole. For supracritical and near-supracritical scalar field scattering on an extremal black hole in $5$ dimensions, we find that the hole remains disconnected from its charged counterpart. Additionally, we discover that in near-extremal and sub-supracritical scalar field scattering, there is an endless supply of energy that flows into the black hole.

We develop an axiomatic framework for non-classical sets within the context of Real Algebraic Geometry and Semicircular Geometry. This framework is guided by the fundamental axiom of anti-classicality, which posits that non-classical sets must be absent from any real closed field extension of the ground field and that their inherent properties cannot be replicated in such extensions. The remaining axioms are then used to characterize these non-classical sets in conjunction with the semi-axioms. As a result, we define the theoretical underpinnings for the existence of structures such as 5-colored Kneser graphs, infinitely large collections, and the Hilbert Hotel within the realm of semicircular geometry.

Utilizing high-quality ECoG brain signals for controlling an external device for locomotion allows researchers to pinpoint exact locations involved in function prediction, an advantage traditional non-invasive EEG cannot offer. This study compares an advanced deep learning model using ECoG data to a conventional EEG prediction framework, which incorporates a new preprocessing technique and feature extraction method. The proposed method matches the prediction accuracy of state-of-the-art EEG models, but successfully reduces training time by up to 50%. Furthermore, the proposed deep learning model achieves the same accuracy as traditional EEG models but with significantly fewer sensors, an advantage traditional EEG models cannot match. The study shows that it is possible to predict complex functions such as stair climbing using ECoG data and an advanced deep learning model, an achievement not possible with traditional EEG models. The proposed method also exhibits greater consistency than previous state-of-the-art EEG prediction frameworks.

Computing entropies and related measures like the Bhattacharyya distance is challenging for distributions without direct evaluability. Probability distributions of integer sequences often fall into this category, particularly those of natural language texts. Although count-based methods like Zipf's law and the PMD have been widely used, they do not accurately represent empirical data. A newer, non-parametric approach called the TD does not make assumptions about specific probability values and provides a flexible framework for deriving probability estimates, entropy, and other metrics. This study compares various entropy and distance computations for probability distributions derived from text data, focusing on methods like the TD, the CD, and the MD. The study shows that both mutual information and Bhattacharyya distance can be accurately computed using the TD based on corpus size, and that the entropy can be accurately computed using a bias-corrected version of the TD's entropy estimator. The study concludes that exact entropy computations are not always feasible, particularly for rare words, and suggests using a maximum likelihood bias correction to accurately compute the total entropy of texts.

Given an right-angled Artin group acting on a tree, we establish conditions under which a subgraph divided into two separate parts can cause the action to fail being an A-tree, for any integer A greater than one.

Dynamic graph classification is a critical task that involves classifying graph nodes based on their substructure and surrounding environment. Existing solutions for this task are often complicated and fail to account for the positional information within the graph. We introduce DECENNT, a novel approach centered on creating an efficient and location-independent node representation through the use of circularly-shifted graph convolution. DECENNT's simplicity, combined with its use of highly localized convolutions, provides a robust solution for processing graphs of various sizes. Our extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of DECENNT, achieving top-class accuracy and surpassing current state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin.

Stochastic processes form the foundation of most contemporary evolutionary models, serving as crucial components in reconstructing phylogeny. Despite their widespread adoption, state-space explosion in genomic data poses a significant challenge in evaluating the likelihood of phylogenetic trees. This research presents an innovative approach for assessing the probability of a given historical tree, incorporating a given sequence of state changes. It achieves this by integrating elements from scalar field theory and geometric analysis of manifolds, resulting in a novel approach that bypasses traditional methods for calculating historical probabilities. The new approach utilizes an integral involving a scalar function's derivative raised to a power, related to a path integral. It yields a solution that is both physically and mathematically coherent, offering an exponential decrease in complexity in relation to the length of a phylogenetic tree. This research proposes a new method for estimating probabilities along phylogenetic trees, drawing on principles from statistical physics and manifold geometry to provide a more efficient alternative to traditional methods such as the Matrix Exponential. It also offers an analysis of the new method's accuracy when applied to DNA sequence evolution on a given historical tree.

The growing number of biological entities in our lives necessitates an efficient method to monitor their movement, encompassing everything from insects to humans. To achieve this goal, the goal-seeking behavior of a goal marker can be employed to distinguish between biological and non-biological entities. Beyond traditional approaches, this paper explores goal-oriented movement patterns to further refine tracking methods. To make this objective, a deep learning network is designed, named G-GoalNet, which predicts whether an entity's movement is goal-directed. G-GoalNet's design incorporates multiple factors, including spatial and temporal information, as well as external input context, to produce an accurate outcome. A public dataset containing diverse types of moving entities is introduced to extensively evaluate and test the proposed approach, resulting in improved results that demonstrate a significant increase in tracking accuracy of about 15%.

The introduction of a variant of the Nested Neumann algorithm with an modified filter factor formula, along with a corresponding bound of $O(1)$ for its convergence rate. The new formula shows the algorithm's inception depth, or the number of nested levels, has a minimal impact on convergence rate, especially with high nestings.

Building on previous work eigenchannel theory for scattering inside confined spaces has been calculated directly from the eigenmodes of the space in question. A calculation has now been made for a two-dimensional rectangular region with randomly polarized eigenmodes. As a result the non-Kerrllian nature of channel eigenstates has been demonstrated for this geometry. It has also been demonstrated that these eigenchannels contain equal amounts of energy on average. Deviations from this average however can be significant. They depend heavily on how the modes fill the space. Universal behavior has been found in relation to the variance of channel eigenvalues and is expressed in terms of the intensity of modes at the boundary. A new method has been found for expressing the relationship between channel eigenvalues and the extent to which modes are localized.

This method enables us to examine specific topological features, such as winding numbers and gaps, at different energy levels. By leveraging our technique, we successfully observed the localization of Anderson insulator band structures containing multiple gaps and identified distinct patterns without knowing their inherent shape. Additionally, our method facilitated an examination of how these features change with varying levels of disorder and allowed us to examine the coherence between different energy levels through andon divergence that occurs near a specific universal rate.

We extend our previous investigation into geometric invariants of genus-one curves by examining the behavior of normalized hitting time invariants under varying parameter inputs. Our expanded analysis employs a set of 22 data points and employs two distinct computational methods. Our results indicate that certain inherent properties of the curves maintain consistent values, yielding similar irreducible polynomials, despite substantial differences in the computation methods. This finding reinforces the concept that a certain inherent structure exists in these curves, with different parts of this structure revealing themselves depending on the method used. Our data also supports the hypothesis that the invariants can be decomposed into two components, with one component representing a universal polynomial that appears in all computations of a given curve, and the other component being an exception that varies between different computations of the same curve.

We have studied the sensitivity of top quark pair productions with extra heavy Higgs bosons $H/A$ at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) for energy levels of 13 and 14 TeV. The cross-section for these productions was calculated using a method that accounts for the asymptotic behavior of QCD, considering four distinct phases of complex parameters $\epsilon_{AB}$. To better understand the topic, we first examined the properties of the complex parameters and the associated complex-dimensional scalars before proceeding with our analysis. The outcomes of this study are dependent on the dimensions $d_A$ and $d_B$ of the vector-like quark pair representations, as well as the phases of the complex parameters $\epsilon_{AB}$. The dimensions $d_A$ and $d_B$ are divided into four phases: (a) $5\leq d_A,d_B<6$, (b) $4.5\leq d_A<5$ and $5\leq d_B<6$, (c) $4.5\leq d_A,d_B<5$, and (d) $5\leq d_A<5.5$ and $5.5\leq d_B<6$.
